voiceInstructions: Warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Relaxed, welcoming and lightly playful, with a gentle smile and conversational rhythm. Keep scientific terms precise and avoid an announcer cadence. Slow down for equations, numbers and conversions. Give brief natural thinking pauses after questions. Do not add words or laughter absent from the script.
title: Rutherford scattering, Bohr atoms and hydrogen spectra

sources.title: NTA: Official JEE Main 2026 syllabus, Physics Unit 18
OpenStax: Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom

chapters.title: A tiny nucleus changes the atomic picture
points: Most alpha particles passed through a thin foil with little deflection.
Rare large-angle deflections indicated concentrated positive charge.
The nucleus contains almost all the atomic mass.
chapters.script: Hey, welcome back. Imagine sending positively charged alpha particles toward an extremely thin metal foil. Most pass through with little change in direction. A small fraction turn sharply, and a very few come back toward the source. Those rare events are the important clue. A diffuse positive charge spread throughout an atom cannot easily produce such strong deflections in this picture. Rutherford's nuclear model puts the positive charge and almost all the mass into a tiny central nucleus. Most of the atomic volume lies outside that nucleus. Please do not interpret the phrase mostly empty space as saying that quantum electron distributions have no physical role. It is a comparison of the very small nuclear size with the much larger atomic size. An alpha particle has charge plus two e, and a nucleus with atomic number Z has charge plus Z e. Their repulsion can bend the alpha particle's path. A particle passing far away feels a smaller deflecting influence than one approaching closely. Think for a moment: which observation supports a small concentrated nucleus most directly? It is the rare large-angle scattering, especially backward scattering, not simply the fact that many particles pass through. The experiment changed the structure we assign to an atom. But a classical planetary model still faces a problem: an accelerating orbiting charge should radiate energy. Bohr's model will introduce new postulates to address atomic stability and discrete spectra.

chapters.title: Closest approach in a head-on collision
chapters.formula: Heavy fixed nucleus: rmin = 2Zke^2/K; ke^2 approximately 1.44 MeV fm
points: At a head-on turning point, initial kinetic energy becomes electric potential energy.
Neglect nuclear recoil and use Coulomb repulsion outside the nucleus.
For Z = 79 and K = 7.2 MeV, rmin = 31.6 fm.
chapters.script: Let's work out one clean scattering case rather than guessing from the picture. An alpha particle approaches a heavy nucleus directly along the line joining their centers. Treat the nucleus as fixed, neglecting recoil. At the closest point of this head-on approach, the alpha particle momentarily stops before moving back. Its initial kinetic energy has become electric potential energy of repulsion. Taking potential energy zero at infinite separation, write K equals k times two e times Z e divided by r minimum. Rearranging gives r minimum equal to two Z k e squared divided by K. The factor two comes from the alpha particle's charge. A useful constant is k e squared approximately one point four four mega electron volts times femtometers. For a gold nucleus, Z is seventy-nine. Let the incident alpha energy be seven point two mega electron volts. The distance is two times seventy-nine times one point four four divided by seven point two, giving thirty-one point six femtometers. That is a center-to-center distance, not the alpha particle's traveled distance. It is outside the approximate gold nuclear radius, so the Coulomb model is sensible for this illustration. Your turn: if incident energy doubles, what happens to this head-on closest distance? It halves. For a non-head-on trajectory, motion has an angular component at closest approach, so you cannot say all kinetic energy has vanished. Use the head-on formula only when that condition is stated.

chapters.title: Bohr states have definite energies
chapters.formula: One-electron ion: En = -13.6 Z^2/n^2 eV; rn = 0.0529 n^2/Z nm
points: Bohr postulated stationary states and L = nh/(2pi).
These formulas apply to hydrogen-like single-electron systems.
Negative energy means bound relative to an electron at infinity.
chapters.script: Bohr kept a nuclear center but added rules that classical motion alone does not supply. Certain stationary states are allowed, and an electron in one of those states does not continuously radiate energy in the model. The angular momentum is restricted to n times h divided by two pi, with n a positive integer. Combining that postulate with Coulomb force providing the centripetal force gives allowed radii and energies. For a hydrogen-like system containing exactly one electron, the energy is minus thirteen point six times Z squared divided by n squared, in electron volts. The radius is zero point zero five two nine times n squared divided by Z, in nanometers. We neglect reduced-mass corrections in these introductory formulas. Negative energy means the electron is bound, with the zero chosen for a separated electron and nucleus. It does not mean negative kinetic energy. For hydrogen, Z is one. At n equal to two, energy is minus three point four electron volts, and radius is zero point two one one six nanometers. Compare helium plus, which also has one electron but Z equal to two. Its ground-state energy is minus fifty-four point four electron volts. The stronger nuclear attraction makes it more tightly bound. Do not apply these simple formulas to neutral helium with two electrons. Also remember that Bohr orbits are a historical model, not the full modern quantum description of electron position. The model's useful predictions here are its energy levels and the resulting spectral frequencies.

chapters.title: A transition emits the energy difference
chapters.formula: Emitted photon energy = Ei - Ef = hc/lambda
points: A downward transition emits; a suitable upward transition absorbs.
Hydrogen n = 3 to n = 2 releases about 1.889 eV.
The corresponding wavelength is about 656 nm.
chapters.script: Now we have levels. How does light enter the story? An electron making a transition from a higher energy level to a lower one emits a photon carrying the difference. Initial energy minus final energy is positive for that downward transition. Do not subtract the magnitudes blindly; write the signed energies first. For hydrogen moving from n equal to three to n equal to two, energy released is thirteen point six times one fourth minus one ninth. That is approximately one point eight eight nine electron volts. Using h c approximately twelve hundred forty electron volt nanometers, divide twelve hundred forty by that energy. The wavelength is about six hundred fifty-six nanometers, a visible Balmer line. Let's compare the transition from two to one. Its photon energy is ten point two electron volts, giving roughly one hundred twenty-two nanometers in the ultraviolet. Larger energy difference means shorter photon wavelength. Pause for a prediction: does an electron at n equal to two need thirteen point six electron volts to be removed completely? No. Its energy is minus three point four, so reaching zero requires three point four electron volts. Thirteen point six is the ground-state ionization energy for hydrogen in this model. For absorption between discrete bound states, the photon must match an allowed energy gap, subject to transition rules. Ionization is different: a photon above the ionization threshold can leave the released electron with surplus kinetic energy. Identify the starting state before choosing a threshold.

chapters.title: Spectral series and line counting
points: Lyman transitions finish at n = 1; Balmer transitions finish at n = 2.
The shortest wavelength in a series is its high-n limit.
An ensemble with levels up to n = 4 can produce six distinct transitions.
chapters.script: Let's organize the spectrum instead of memorizing isolated colors. A spectral series groups transitions that finish at the same lower level. Lyman lines finish at one and lie in the ultraviolet for hydrogen. Balmer lines finish at two. Paschen lines finish at three and lie in the infrared for hydrogen. The Rydberg relation gives inverse wavelength as R H times Z squared times the difference between inverse squared lower and higher quantum numbers. Use the lower index first so the bracket is positive. In a given emission series, increasing the starting level makes the photon energy approach a limiting value. The shortest wavelength is the series limit, not the first line. For hydrogen's Balmer limit, the photon energy approaches three point four electron volts, giving roughly three hundred sixty-five nanometers with our rounded constants. Now a different kind of JEE question: an ensemble of excited hydrogen atoms can make transitions among levels one through four. How many distinct energy differences are possible? Count pairs. Four times three divided by two gives six. That does not mean one electron emits all six photons during a single downward cascade. An individual cascade follows one route and can contain at most three downward steps from four to one. Across many atoms and different routes, the six transition energies can appear. More detailed quantum transition selection rules are outside this simple counting exercise. Finish by checking the lower series level, the energy sign, and whether a question refers to one cascade or an ensemble.

quiz.question: Which foil-scattering observation most directly supports a concentrated positive nucleus?
quiz.explanation: Strong rare deflections require concentrated positive charge in the Rutherford model.

quiz.question: For a head-on alpha approach to fixed Z = 79, K = 7.2 MeV and ke^2 = 1.44 MeV fm, rmin is:
Hydrogen's Bohr energy at n = 2 is:
Hydrogen's n = 2 Bohr radius, with a0 = 0.0529 nm, is:
The hydrogen n = 3 to n = 2 emission wavelength is approximately:
quiz.explanation: Delta E = 13.6(1/4 - 1/9) eV; lambda = 1240/Delta E, approximately 656 nm.

quiz.question: In the simple all-pairs model, an ensemble with levels up to n = 4 can produce how many distinct lines?
quiz.explanation: 4(4-1)/2 = 6 possible transition pairs, not six photons in a single cascade.
